To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the srf-3 virus is cholesterol independent, that the srf3 mutant is dependent on the cholesterol concentration in the cell, and that the mutation that confers the cholesterol independent phenotype occurs at position 226 of the E1 subunit of the SFV spike protein.
a single amino acid mutation in the alphavirus E1 spike protein confers a cholesterol-independent phenotype for both membrane fusion, and exit from infected cells.
we have identified a single point mutation that controls the cholesterol requirement of both membrane fusion and virus egress.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis of membrane fusion, which is the process that allows enveloped viruses to infect cells.
the role of cholesterol and the viral E1 protein in membrane fusion and the exit of Semliki forest virus.
the molecular mechanisms of virus entry and exit and the role of cellular membranes and membrane lipids in these processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cholesterol requirement of SFV is a consequence of the cholesterol dependence of the virus spike proteins.
a single point mutation in the SFV E1 spike protein controls the cholesterol dependence of SFV entry and exit.
a single mutation in the SFV E1 protein can alter the virus cholesterol dependence, and this mutation is in a region of the protein that has previously been shown to affect the fusion process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the srf-3 mutation is a gain of function mutation, which increases the cholesterol independence of SFV membrane fusion and budding, and that it does this by altering the conformation of the spike protein.
we identify a cholesterol binding pocket in the SFV E1 spike protein, and that this binding pocket is important for both fusion and exit.
a single point mutation in the SFV spike protein can control the cholesterol dependence of both membrane fusion and virus release.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cholesterol is required for efficient SFV exit, which is a new finding.
a single amino acid mutation in SFV E1 protein can change the cholesterol dependence of both fusion and exit, suggesting a direct link between fusion and budding.
